keyQuestions.text: How do OpenBot and the other reference repos give a team conversations with a bot and an activity feed, and can a terminal or TUI match the OpenBot desktop app for that, or is a desktop shell such as Tauri worth adding?

How do approvals work in OpenBot and the other repos, and what is the smallest small-team model of who can talk to, approve for and change a bot, compared with skilled bots' needs-you items and run records?
How does a terminal or TUI present a conversation with a bot together with its approvals, activity and routine list, and which repo's terminal frontend is worth copying?
How are conversations persisted and fanned out so several bots can share one thread, and what is the smallest activity record that can be shown after the fact?
What is the smallest sign-in and role model for a few people sharing one machine or host, and which parts of OpenBot's owner/admin/member split and turnstone's RBAC can be dropped?
How should shared versus per-person memory be scoped when a few people use the same bots, and what does OpenBot's memory model do that skilled bots' per-bot files do not?

keyFindings.text: A terminal precedent already exists in the reference set. openhuman ships `openhuman-tui`, a conversation-first terminal frontend built with ratatui and crossterm that embeds the core in-process with no HTTP server or sidecar; it covers login, saved conversations, model and agent selection, approvals, tools, child-run inspection and diagnostics. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/openhuman-main/crates/openhuman-tui/README.md:3-9]

OpenBot Desktop is a Tauri 2 shell whose responsibilities are the machine around the bot, not the chat itself: the manifest depends on `tauri` with `tray-icon` and `image-png`, and the entry point's module list covers install, engine, stack, update, host folder access, telemetry, recorder and uninstall. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/desktop/src-tauri/Cargo.toml:28] [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/desktop/src-tauri/src/main.rs:13-31]

OpenBot frames a bot as eight primitives in four pairs, and Conversations and Activity are the two ends of the work loop: Conversations is "How do I give it work?", Activity is "What did it do?". The order is fixed: Conversations, Routines, Memory, Skills, Apps, Computer, Approvals, Activity. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/how-openbot-works.md:6-18] [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/how-openbot-works.md:168]

OpenBot supports several bots in one conversation. The group chat is a server-owned shared transcript: the person posts once, `@Name` addresses one bot, otherwise every addressed bot runs through the ordinary headless AG-UI path one after another, and each bot answers in a thread of its own that the UI draws attributed. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/app/src/components/channels/group-chat.tsx:42-48]

OpenBot's activity pane is a lifecycle view, not a raw log: entries are typed as `routine`, `responsibility`, `handoff` and related kinds, each with its own icon and label, and the pane links back to the routine, task or conversation that produced the entry. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/app/src/components/bot-profile/activity.tsx:67-79] [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/how-openbot-works.md:141-154]

Skilled bots today has no conversation surface at all. The `bots` CLI is a one-verb front door over the runtime: `run`, `disable`, `enable`, `pause`, `resume`, `inbox`, `enqueue`, `drain`, `schedule`, `answer`, `status`. The nearest thing to a conversation is `answer <item-id> <text>`, which answers a needs-you item and queues the run that continues it; the nearest thing to an activity feed is `status`, which shows each installed bot's last run, delivery and open needs-you items from the status index. [SOURCE: .skilled/bin/bots.cjs:19-50]

That TUI is a real host, not a wrapper: its event loop folds the same `web_chat` broadcast stream the desktop app consumes into `TranscriptState`, alongside a crossterm keyboard reader and a spinner ticker. The README documents `/sessions`, `/resume`, `/permissions`, `/skills`, `/mcp` and `/artifacts` as first-class commands, plus a persistent attention control for pending approvals and plan review. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/openhuman-main/crates/openhuman-tui/src/app.rs:8-10] [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/openhuman-main/crates/openhuman-tui/README.md:94-107]

The other reference repos split between desktop shells and web apps: OpenMausBot is an Electron app described as "a local-first chat app for running a team of AI agents"; OpenGhost is Electron with its own hand-written UI; buzz ships a Tauri desktop plus web and admin-web; hermes-muse ships a dashboard plugin rather than an app; rakazo carries desktop, mobile, web, www, api and worker apps in one workspace. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenMausBot-main/package.json:5] [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenMausBot-main/package.json:169] [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenGhost-main/package.json:6] [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/buzz-main/desktop/package.json:19-25] [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/buzz-main/desktop/package.json:53-55] [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/hermes-muse-main/desktop/plugin.js:1]

Verdict on terminal versus desktop for this pair: a TUI can carry all four surfaces the question names — conversations, an approvals inbox, an activity feed and a routine list — because each is text-first and event-driven, and openhuman proves the shape. What a Tauri shell adds is the machine around the terminal: a native window and tray, self-update, OS folder pickers that can grant scoped file authority, microphone capture, and supervision of a local engine or container stack. A small team that already runs the bots CLI on one machine or a shared host does not need those on day one. [INFERENCE: based on findings 2-8]

`bots answer` is the continuation path: it records the operator's answer on the item, enqueues one `resume` request keyed by the item id, then advances the generation stamp. The answer is written before the enqueue so the resumed run is not refused, a duplicate answer stores one request, and the text is checked for secret literals before storage because it reaches the resumed prompt. [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/runtime/lib/answer.ts:3-17]

An approval card offers four answers: Allow once, Allow for this conversation (same bot, same tool, same place, same account; it does not reach another conversation, bot or tool), Always allow here (saved as a personal rule), and Deny. An allow reaches only the kind of action it was given on: allowing an ordinary click never opens that site's Send or Place order button. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/approvals.md:21-31]

Bot ownership and visibility are separate from conversation membership. A person-made bot is owned by that person and package bots are ownerless; visibility is `private` (owner and administrators) or `public` (everyone in the deployment); publishing a Team Bot to people or groups is a separate, revocable record that does not change the bot's own visibility. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/coworkers.md:17-21] [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/coworkers.md:53-58]

OpenBot decides whether to ask with an ordered policy, first match wins: (1) kinds of action — deleting, sending, sharing, posting, paying, changing a password or account settings — ask in every edition by default; (2) rules, where the strictest matching rule wins, so a team rule that asks beats a personal allowance; (3) auto-review when turned on; (4) Extra vigilant, a personal switch that is off unless enabled. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/approvals.md:3-14]

OpenBot's role vocabulary is exactly three: owner, admin and member. A single function decides administration (`role === "admin" || role === "owner"`), an unknown role is read as member, and the server enforces auth and roles independently of the app. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/app/src/lib/auth/roles.ts:1-26] [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/architecture.md:418]

Skilled bots' approval is definition-level, not action-level. An unattended run — a scheduled fire, a queued request, a resume — runs only the exact bytes an operator approved: a hash of `BOT.md` and the repository's `bots/config.json`, kept under the user-level state root where no run can write it, and written only when an operator installs a schedule, enables a bot, or runs a bot by hand. A manual run is never refused for drift, because typing it is the approval. [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/runtime/lib/approval.ts:3-16]

Skilled bots' needs-you item is the human-decision primitive: an unattended run that needs a decision ends instead of waiting and leaves one item under the user-level state root so a run can neither forge nor clear it. Its state (open, answered, expired) is derived from its fields on every read and never stored, so it cannot disagree with them. [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/runtime/lib/needs-you.ts:3-12]

Skilled bots' run record is the join every later surface reads: the queue links a request to its run through it, delivery appends to it, and the status index is built from it. It lives under the user-level state root, and `awaiting-decision` is a terminal exit for a run that parked a question. [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/runtime/lib/run-record.ts:3-12]

Smallest small-team model: skilled bots needs no sign-in system and no owner/admin/member split. It needs one operator identity that is recorded on the acts that already exist — the needs-you answer, the definition approval, the run record — plus one visibility rule per bot (who may run it) and one shared-vs-personal memory scope. OpenBot's owner/admin/member and turnstone's RBAC are both more than a few people on one machine or a shared host require; the part worth copying is the ordered policy (kinds, then rules, then a personal strictness switch), not the role tree. [INFERENCE: based on findings 1-11]

The personal edition is the smallest possible identity model: one person on their own machine, nobody signs in, one computer, and a single Personal Assistant bot. With no identity provider the server refuses to start unless `OPENBOT_SINGLE_USER=true` declares every request the one fixed administrator, and it still refuses a public address. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/personal-edition.md:3-8] [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/architecture.md:427]

The team edition adds an administrator control per action kind with three settings: Members choose (the default four answers), Ask every time (Allow once and Deny only, and prior allowances for that kind stop applying), and Members do it themselves (the bot never performs it; the person gets "I did it myself" and "Don't do it"). [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/approvals.md:56-67]

Turnstone is the enterprise-shaped version of the same idea: RBAC with admin, operator and viewer roles, plus admin-defined tool policies with `allow`, `deny` and `ask` actions and first-match priority. It is more machinery than a few people need, but the three-word policy vocabulary is the cleanest statement of what an approval layer does. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/turnstone-main/docs/governance.md:9-30] [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/turnstone-main/docs/governance.md:40-52]

`bots status` joins three sources — status index rows, install records and `launchctl print` — and classifies each bot row through a fixed state order: retired, missing, unreadable, needs-reinstall, held, launchd-failed, run-folder-gone, unknown. That vocabulary can back an activity feed without inventing a new one. [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/runtime/lib/status.ts:3-14] [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/runtime/lib/status.ts:48-58]

Decisions are overlays with single-key answers. The plan-review overlay draws the summary and numbered steps and states its keys inline: "a approve · r reject · e request revision · Esc leaves pending". Pending approvals and plan review share one persistent attention control. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/openhuman-main/crates/openhuman-tui/src/app/overlays.rs:14-27] [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/openhuman-main/crates/openhuman-tui/README.md:94]

Its secondary views are drawn as plain text rows and buttons in the same frame: `config` lists editable rows with a selected marker and a hint line, `settings` and `logs` follow the same pattern. A terminal UI does not need a widget toolkit beyond rows, a selection cursor and a detail pane. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/openhuman-main/crates/openhuman-tui/src/render/views.rs:2-56] [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/openhuman-main/crates/openhuman-tui/src/render/views.rs:57-175]

OpenBot's approval is drawn inline in the conversation where the action would have happened, read from the same owner-scoped inbox as the Approvals page, so a decision made in either place is the one decision; after the decision the server runs the action exactly once and continues the conversation. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/app/src/components/approvals/inline-approval.tsx:20-27]

OpenBot's approval page is a row board with a per-row menu, and a conversation's waiting question is a questionnaire with progress and next/previous navigation. Both are list-plus-detail shapes that a terminal can reproduce with rows and keys. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/app/src/components/approvals/waiting.tsx:1-40] [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/app/src/components/approvals/question-notice.tsx:37-60]

OpenBot's routines are one list, and every row is the same sentence in four parts: What it is, Starts, Does, Until. The page merges routines, goals and check-ins on read even though they are three server stores. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/routines.md:3-28]

openhuman-tui's main screen is exactly two regions: a chat transcript and a bottom-anchored composer. Everything else is a tab or overlay, not a second window. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/openhuman-main/crates/openhuman-tui/src/render.rs:142-264]

Skilled bots' status index is already the data source an activity or routine list needs: a derived SQLite file under the user-level state root, built only from run records and needs-you items, readable without opening a run folder, with run rows written once and never updated. [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/runtime/lib/status-index.ts:3-14]

Smallest change: one `bots chat` (or `bots tui`) command that renders three panes from files the runtime already writes — transcript from run records and the parked-run prompt, approvals from `bots inbox`, routines from the installed schedule records — plus one overlay for a needs-you answer. No daemon, no database beyond the status index, and no new state. [INFERENCE: based on findings 1-9]

The frontend worth copying is openhuman-tui. Turnstone's "console" is a web cluster dashboard that subscribes to node SSE streams and reverse-proxies node UIs, not a terminal frontend; OpenGhost and OpenMausBot are Electron apps whose UI code is not portable to a terminal. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/turnstone-main/docs/console.md:3-20]

The TUI turns app surfaces into slash commands rather than screens: `/sessions`, `/permissions`, `/skills`, `/mcp`, `/artifacts`, `/diff`, `/review`, `/usage`, `/status`, `/settings`, `/config`. This is the concrete recipe for giving a CLI an approvals inbox and an activity feed without building pages. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/openhuman-main/crates/openhuman-tui/README.md:103-107]

A group message carries more than text: `personId` or `botId` as its author, a status, `answeredBy`, a `consent` record naming bot and server, and optional attachments. That is enough to draw an attributed multi-bot thread and to show which bot answered a question a person was asked. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/app/src/lib/groups.ts:53-72] [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/app/src/lib/groups.ts:102-104]

Every request producer writes the same record shape, so one drain reads one shape and dedupe works the same way for all of them. The idempotency key comes from the event source and that source's event id (or a caller key), never from a hash of the body, and the request id is derived from the bot and the key so a re-sent event names the request already queued. [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/runtime/lib/request-record.ts:3-18]

Fan-out is per-bot threads on the server, not one agent with many voices: each addressed bot runs the ordinary headless AG-UI path and the shared transcript is the assembly of their answers, with `@Name` addressing one bot and no address meaning every bot in turn. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/app/src/components/channels/group-chat.tsx:42-48]

Gap: no grouping view. The status index has per-bot row states but no needs_you/working/scheduled/done/stopped/failed/recurring grouping; the smallest change is a projection over run records and needs-you items that reuses OpenBot's seven group ids and its pure grouping rule. [INFERENCE: based on findings 4-5]

Gap: skilled bots has no transcript store. A conversation today is a chain of runs (request, run record, delivery), not a message log; the smallest change is a conversation id on the request plus one message row per human message, bot delivery and answer, written by the same atomic state writer the queue already uses. [INFERENCE: based on findings 5-7]

OpenBot persists a group conversation as a channel with members and messages read through the conversations API: `listConversationMembers`, `listConversationMessages` and `sendConversationMessage`, with the transcript capped at the newest 200 lines. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/app/src/lib/groups.ts:10-31] [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/app/src/lib/groups.ts:136-139]

OpenBot's activity grouping is a pure function over two reads: the bot's activity (routines, goals, hand-offs, follow-ups, questions) and the person's tasks. Each entry lands in exactly one group, in this order: needs_you, working, scheduled, done, stopped, failed, recurring; an empty group is omitted. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/app/src/lib/bot-lifecycle/activity-groups.ts:6-45]

Reuse: OpenBot is MIT-licensed, and `activity-groups.ts` is a small pure module whose only imports are types and two helpers, so its grouping rule can be lifted with attribution rather than re-derived. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/LICENSE:1-3] [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/package.json:4]

Skilled bots already persists most of what an activity record needs. A run record holds the request join (request id, lease nonce, result event id, fired slot, resumed item), a dispatch snapshot (source, scheduled time, dispatch time, lateness, skipped and held slots), the budget (declared and measured), the exit (reason, failure class, needs-you item), evidence locations (run folder, ledger, receipts, worktree) and delivery entries. [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/runtime/lib/run-record.ts:70-190]

The queue is a file queue under the user-level state root, keyed by repository identity, where every state change is one rename between sibling folders so two consumers can never claim the same request. A seen-key marker turns a re-sent event into a duplicate, a crash after the marker loses the event rather than running it twice, and a request is quarantined after three attempts. [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/runtime/lib/request-queue.ts:3-25]

Everything a run must not be able to write lives in a user-level state root outside every checkout, owner-only (`0o700`), and the state root an installed job carries in its environment outranks the checkout's config so a run with write access cannot redirect switches, holds or leases. [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/runtime/lib/state-root.ts:3-25] [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/runtime/lib/state-root.ts:29-38]

Gap: skilled bots records no actor anywhere. A definition approval records the source kind (`install`, `enable`, `manual-run`) but not who did it; a needs-you answer records text and time but not who answered; a run record has no requester field. Adding one `actor` string to those three records is the smallest change that makes the model above real. [INFERENCE: based on findings 1 and 2] [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/runtime/lib/approval.ts:29-36]

OpenBot's administrative model is a floor plus delegation: `INITIAL_ADMIN_EMAILS` always makes an address an administrator, everybody else's role is decided on the People screen, every change writes an audit row, SCIM can provision people, and removing somebody deletes their sessions and denies their address. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/architecture.md:420-430]

OpenBot's sign-in is enterprise-shaped by design: Google, Microsoft or Okta from the environment plus SAML and OpenID Connect providers registered at runtime and routed by email domain; one resolver answers both "whose threads are these" and "which bots may they run", so the two can never disagree. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/architecture.md:418-419]

OpenBot's single-user fallback is one flag plus an address restriction: with no identity provider the server refuses to start unless `OPENBOT_SINGLE_USER=true` declares every request the one fixed administrator, and it still refuses to start when any configured public URL resolves to a public address; loopback is silent and a private address is allowed with a warning. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/architecture.md:427]

OpenGhost uses three permission modes per session — Ask, Auto, Full access — rather than user roles. It is a posture chosen for the work, not an identity, and it is the cheapest way to express "this bot may act freely in its own folder but must ask outside it". [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenGhost-main/README.md:155]

OpenMausBot states the same posture skilled bots already has: local-first, bring-your-own-agent, no cloud requirement. None of the reference repos that target one person adds a sign-in system. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenMausBot-main/README.md:9]

Skilled bots has no person identity at all. Its identity is the repository, `owner/name`, resolved in a fixed order — an installed job's pinned environment value, then `bots/config.json`, then the environment and the git origin — and an unknown identity is a refusal, never a fallback, so two unknown repositories can never share state. [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/runtime/lib/identity.ts:3-24] [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/runtime/lib/identity.ts:52-76]

Smallest model for a few people on one machine or host: no sign-in service. Take the operator's identity from the host the team already trusts (OS user, SSH key, or a `--as <name>` flag on the CLI), record it on the three acts that matter (definition approval, needs-you answer, run record), and add one optional read-only viewer. Per-bot permission becomes one list of names or a group, checked when a run is enqueued or an answer is accepted. [INFERENCE: based on findings 1-8]

Turnstone's minimal useful shape is three roles — admin, operator, viewer — with granular permission strings and API tokens, plus tool policies that decide allow, deny or ask per tool pattern. The roles are more than a small team needs; the read-only/operator split is the part worth keeping. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/turnstone-main/docs/governance.md:9-30]

Learning containers are per person, not per bot: a recording joins the person's own container, a run draws the bot's own published skills first, then the person's, then any skill another person opened, and each person chooses sharing (own bots only, every bot in the deployment, or skill by skill). [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/automatic-learning.md:50-58]

OpenBot keeps the provenance record that its memory backend lacks — where a memory came from, its review state, which bot formed it and which source imported it — and applies it before a bot sees anything: a bot-formed memory reaches only the forming bot while it holds the source app, and every call is user-scope with project-scoped results dropped, so one person's bot never sees another person's memory. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/architecture.md:377-383]

OpenBot splits memory by origin, not by scope picker: facts the person adds are shared with all their bots, while facts a bot picks up while working stay with that bot. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/how-openbot-works.md:61-62]

OpenBot's personal memory exists only in the team edition. The personal edition has none at all: OpenBot Desktop's local Intelligence is licensed without memory, so there the memory has no screens, routes, tools or sources. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/architecture.md:370-375]

OpenBot's skills-from-use is a separate learning loop, not memory: completed conversations feed a Learning container, Intelligence proposes skills with their SKILL.md, the reason and the conversations they were learned from, and a person approves or rejects. In the team edition nothing — not a scheduled analysis, not enabling Learning — approves a skill by itself. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/automatic-learning.md:3-5] [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/automatic-learning.md:30-35]

Openhuman's memory is the service-shaped opposite: recall, fetch and store over a pluggable engine, stored in CortexDB, with memory off entirely when no engine is configured. That is a dependency a small team does not need. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/openhuman-main/docs/gitbooks/en/developing/architecture.md:225]

Skilled bots' BOT.md schema has no memory field. A definition is id, trigger, runtime, budget, enabled, delivery, posture, precheck, specFolder and body; memory is not part of the contract. [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/runtime/lib/definition.ts:23-58]

Smallest change for skilled bots: memory as typed files, not a service. Per-bot memory at `bots/<id>/memory.md` and shared memory at `bots/memory.md`, each entry carrying type (user, general, feedback, reference) and provenance (actor, source, bot, date); `bots remember` appends and `bots memory` lists; the runner prepends both files to the prompt. Skills from use stay in the spec-kit loop: a proposed `SKILL.md` is written into a packet's scratch area and reviewed like any other skill, with no Learning service. [INFERENCE: based on findings 2-9]

The bots runtime has 28 flat modules and none of them is memory; the modules cover contracts and state, schedule, runner and dispatch, isolation and delivery, the request pipeline, the launchd installer and the status index. Memory is simply not a runtime concern today. [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/runtime/lib/README.md:1-16] [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/runtime/lib/README.md:30-50]

Turnstone's structured memory is the cleanest small model in the reference set: four types (user, general, feedback, reference), five scopes (global, workstream, user, coordinator, project), an identity tuple of name, scope and scope id, upsert on the same identity, and a body-free metadata index at the first turn with an explicit get to read a body. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/turnstone-main/docs/memory.md:1-40]

An OpenBot routine is one sentence in four parts: What (the instruction), Starts (a time, an event, or now once), Does (act, or only tell), Until (you stop it, or an outcome is reached). Goals and check-ins are the same list: a goal is a routine with an outcome, a check-in is a routine that only tells you. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/routines.md:12-28]

Event starts are subscriptions, not triggers in the bot file: a goal carries `subscriptions: {source, eventType}[]`, and a goal runs when asked or when an event wakes it. That is why OpenBot can offer "when a pull request opens" and "when a new email arrives" without a per-bot trigger list. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/app/src/lib/routines/plan.ts:20-32] [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/routines.md:73-77]

Mapping the four parts onto skilled bots: What → the BOT.md body; Starts at a time → a `cron` trigger; Starts when something happens → a `queue` trigger fed by a producer (git-hook already writes one for commits; mail and pull-request events need a small producer that calls `bots enqueue`); Does act → the run; Does only tell → `delivery: local-only`; Until you stop it → the `disabled` switch; Until an outcome → no equivalent today. The smallest change is one optional `until:` block in BOT.md (an outcome sentence plus a check command) and a runner rule that parks or stops the bot when the check passes; the routine list itself is a read over BOT.md files plus the status index. [INFERENCE: based on findings 1-9]

Missed windows are skipped, not replayed: the next run is a stamp, and a deployment that was offline for a month advances the stamp occurrence by occurrence without firing the backlog. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/routines.md:137-145]

OpenBot bounds standing work on purpose: a routine may fire at most every 15 minutes, a person may have at most 20 routines switched on, and both limits exist because a conversation is an easy place to accumulate work without noticing. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/routines.md:110-120]

Skilled bots' cron path is exact by construction: every cron string either becomes launchd calendar dictionaries that fire exactly as cron would, or is refused with a named invariant id; the translator is the only cron reader in the hub, so the checker, installer and slot lister cannot disagree. [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/runtime/lib/cron-translator.ts:3-20]

Skilled bots' trigger vocabulary is already four kinds — cron, queue, git-hook and manual — with git-hook opt-in per repository (`gitHookTrigger`), and only a cron trigger can be installed as a schedule. [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/runtime/lib/definition.ts:25-38] [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/runtime/lib/repo-config.ts:50-51] [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/runtime/lib/installer.ts:585-586]

The fatigue rule is about worth, not retries: a routine posts exactly one message about a failure (the first after a success), ten consecutive failures switch it off, and turning it back on restarts the count. The doc explicitly separates this from the queue's attempt count. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/routines.md:122-135]

The form-to-plan mapping is the executable version of that sentence. `planRoutine` returns exactly three shapes: a routine (act on a schedule, no outcome), a goal (act with an outcome, an event start, or run once) with an optional schedule and a `runNow` flag, or a check-in (tell only, with an interval). [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/app/src/lib/routines/plan.ts:14-40]

The queue drain is a strict router, which is what a routine list needs behind it: claim by rename, quarantine a refusal and never retry it, quarantine a request for a paused or held bot rather than replaying it later, retry a failure to a bound of three, and stop the pass on a setup fault with the claimed request put back. [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/runtime/lib/request-drain.ts:3-20]

A folder on the person's machine is read-only by default and the desktop asks before every edit or command in it; access ends when OpenBot stops, the desktop goes offline, or the person revokes it, and the token is minted on every Start. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/personal-edition.md:129-142]

Code Mode is the house path for external MCP tools: TypeScript execution with on-demand tool loading, used for every external MCP call rather than native tool calls. [SOURCE: .devin/skills/mcp-code-mode/SKILL.md:1-20]

Connector credentials are stored through a credential vault and referenced by id, never inline in YAML; the encryption key must be a base64 32-byte value, and a vault read or decryption fault stops an OAuth client lookup without registering a replacement client. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/architecture.md:414] [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/architecture.md:428]

Every MCP call checks the grant first, then evaluates the same action policy engine with MCP context, then audits the result. The policy engine is shared with ordinary actions, so an approval rule does not need a second implementation for MCP. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/architecture.md:341]

Mapping and smallest change: apps map to MCP servers reached through Code Mode, but there is no grant table and no vault. The smallest change is one `bots vault` surface backed by the OS keychain (or an age-encrypted file), a per-bot allowlist of secret names, and a vault reference syntax in BOT.md; folder access is already a worktree plus a path allowlist, and the executor sandbox already provides the read-only posture. [INFERENCE: based on findings 1-11]

OpenBot governs app access at the administrator level because apps reach external systems with stored credentials: an administrator adds and switches on every app, and a bot's owner may give an app to a bot they own only where an administrator opened it to owners. A grant always uses the asking person's own account, not the owner's. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/architecture.md:325-335]

OpenBot's computer is a browser, a command line and files that stay between tasks, plus folders on the person's own machine. It signs in with a login from the vault that fills the page without the bot reading it, and a step that needs the person (a passkey, a phone code) is taken over by the person and handed back. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/how-openbot-works.md:78-84]

Secret handling is a literal scanner plus an environment allowlist: dispatch collects known secrets from the environment and the repository's dotenv files (minimum length eight), refuses a prompt that contains one, and filters the child environment to the keys the executor kind admits; a needs-you answer is checked the same way before storage. [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/runtime/lib/dispatch.ts:54-57] [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/runtime/lib/dispatch.ts:244-252]

Skilled bots' computer is a worktree: a bot declaring `isolation: worktree` edits in a tree of its own, so an unattended run never writes into the operator's working tree. The tree comes from sk-git's numbering script under a lock, sits outside the checkout and outside the Skilled tree, and links shared paths instead of installing them. [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/runtime/lib/posture.ts:3-14]

The vault belongs to the person, not to a bot: it holds saved logins and keys, apps and the computer both draw on it, and neither keeps secrets of its own, so there is one place to look for a secret, change it or remove it. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/how-openbot-works.md:105-111]

[SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/configuration.md:1500-1524]

An OpenBot skill is a named way of doing a task, called with `/`, and it is made in exactly three ways: the person writes it, the bot records the steps from a demonstration, or OpenBot proposes one from conversations. OpenBot narrows the tools a run is offered by skill: a bot holding more than a handful of tools is offered, per run, only the tools of the skills that match the message. A skill declares the tools it needs, and the declaration grants nothing because the offer is intersected with what the bot was already granted. Gap table, activity: OpenBot has one audit row per decision and a typed lifecycle view; skilled bots has a run record per run, delivery entries, a result event and a status index. The storage is comparable and in one respect stronger (the authorized, idempotent ledger); the gap is a read surface. The smallest change is one `bots activity` read over run records, delivery entries and result events, grouped with OpenBot's seven group ids. [INFERENCE: based on findings 3-7]

Gap table, approvals: OpenBot gates actions against a policy engine with four answer kinds; skilled bots gates definitions before dispatch and parks human decisions as needs-you items. Skilled bots has no per-action gate and no allowance that survives a conversation. The smallest change is not a policy engine: it is a decision row on the run record for each parked question (item id, question, answer, actor, time), which makes the existing needs-you path auditable. [INFERENCE: based on findings 1-2 and 6-7]

OpenBot distinguishes activity from the record: activity is read from the conversation's own tool results, keeps no copy of its own, and is a window; the audit trail is server-side, survives restarts, and is what an investigation reads. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/architecture.md:172]

OpenBot's Activity surface covers everything allowed, refused and failed, appears in Settings for one person and Admin for a team, and a single bot's activity opens from its page beside what it is working on. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/how-openbot-works.md:139-154]

OpenBot's audit trail is written before the action: every tool call returns through a gateway that resolves the target, decides it against the configured policy, writes an audit row, and only then acts — or refuses and names the rule. An action held for a person's approval writes its row when the person answers, and a forwarded action that fails writes a second row. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/architecture.md:7] [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/architecture.md:41-52]

Skilled bots' delivery is at most once and separates run outcome from delivery outcome: a send is claimed before it is made, an uncertain result is recorded `unknown` and never retried, delivery starts only after the terminal run record is written, and a message carries the bot id, run id, outcome, evidence pointers, a kept worktree and a needs-you question — never a command line or an environment value, and a body holding a known secret is withheld. [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/runtime/lib/delivery.ts:3-18]

Skilled bots' result ledger is one result event per run written through the append gateway, validated, authorized and idempotent, so a retry of a failed write is a replay of the same event rather than a second dispatch. [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/runtime/lib/result-ledger.ts:3-14]

Verdict: skilled bots' record is already audit-grade for a single machine. Its two real gaps in this pair are the actor on a decision and a view over the record; neither needs a database, a server, or a new store. [INFERENCE: based on findings 1-9]
**Enterprise identity (SSO, SAML, SCIM):** needs a directory and a second population of users to administer; a few people already have OS or SSH identity (finding 2, iteration 5).
**Kubernetes and Helm:** needs a cluster, a rollout policy and a backup operator; a launchd job and a file queue already provide scheduling and retry on one host (findings 3 and 7).
**Managed upgrades:** needs a vendor relationship and a licence service; the status index and the installer already report versions and install state (findings 4 and 7).
**Mobile:** needs a second client, an app store release cycle and a 12-month compatibility promise; a terminal client runs on the same host as the bots (finding 5).

**Multi-tenant organizations:** needs a server that serves several customers and a database that enforces membership; skilled bots has one checkout and one state root per repository identity (findings 1 and 7).

Enterprise identity is a stack, not a setting: SSO through Google, Microsoft or Okta plus runtime SAML and OIDC providers, SCIM provisioning with a bearer token, a permanent administrator floor, and removal that deletes sessions and denies the address. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/architecture.md:419-430]

Kubernetes is a first-class release target with its own operator tooling: a Helm chart, a promotion command that verifies chart checksums and image digests, migration preflight, quiescence, a required verified backup, and per-release values. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/kubernetes-upgrades.md:1-30]

Managed upgrades are a service relationship: the chart installs a management agent that enrolls with a team licence, heartbeats every minute over mutual TLS, and can let the vendor run upgrades — with an explicit opt-out and a documented list of what leaves the cluster. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/managed-upgrades.md:1-30]

Mobile is a separate product with its own compatibility burden: a React Native app styled with Uniwind and HeroUI Native that must tolerate every server released in the last 12 months and hide features the deployment does not offer. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/mobile/AGENTS.md:1-10]

Multi-tenancy is structural in OpenBot, not a switch: every API resource lives under `/api/v2/organizations/{organizationId}/...`, a deployment holds more than one organization only when `OPENBOT_ORGANIZATION_AUTHORITY` is `intelligence-platform` or `ops`, and a caller who is not a member gets `ORGANIZATION_NOT_FOUND` — the same answer as for an organization that does not exist. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/architecture.md:31]

Skilled bots' deployment model is the opposite end: a per-user launchd job, a user-level state root outside every checkout, a file queue and a derived SQLite index — no server, no database, no tenant, no network listener. [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/runtime/lib/state-root.ts:3-12]

ruledOutDirections.text: Counting "which repo has a desktop app" as evidence of a better conversation surface. Electron and Tauri shells in this set mostly wrap the same web UI; the differentiator is the host contract (streaming events, approvals, sessions), not the window toolkit.

Looking for a ratatui, bubbletea, textual or ink TUI in every reference repo: only openhuman ships a real terminal frontend (`crates/openhuman-tui`). OpenGhost and OpenMausBot are Electron; buzz and OpenBot are Tauri; hermes-muse is a Hermes dashboard plugin; turnstone and rakazo are web/api workspaces. Repeating this survey per repo would add no new signal.

Treating the OpenBot desktop app as the parity target for conversations: its chat UI is the same web app served to the browser, and the Tauri layer's distinctive work is engine/stack management, not chat.
Using OpenBot's mobile app as a comparison point. It is explicitly on the topic's skip list.
Copying OpenBot's owner/admin/member roles into skilled bots. With no sign-in and no tenant, the roles have nothing to distinguish; the same protection comes from recording who approved what.
Copying turnstone's full RBAC and permission-string model. It exists to let an administrator delegate across many users and endpoints, a problem a small team does not have.
Looking for an action-level approval hook in skilled bots' runner. The runtime's only pre-execution gate is the definition hash; there is no per-tool policy layer to extend.
Treating `bots answer` as an approval system. It continues a parked run; it does not gate an action before it happens.
Using OpenBot's admin "Members do it themselves" setting as a template for a role system. It is a per-action-kind switch, not a role.
Building a web UI first. Every surface the question names is a list or a transcript, and the runtime already stores both; a browser adds a server and a session layer without adding information.
Copying OpenGhost's hand-written drawing engine or OpenMausBot's Electron shell. Both are large UI codebases tied to a desktop runtime.
Copying turnstone-console. It solves multi-node cluster visibility, a problem this team does not have.
Looking for a routine list in openhuman-tui: it has `/sessions` and `/skills` but no routine concept; OpenBot's four-part row is the better source.
Searching openhuman-tui for a separate approvals screen: approvals are overlays and a status control, not a page. The overlay is the model to copy.

Building a server-side group transcript with per-bot threads, as OpenBot does. Skilled bots runs one bot per dispatch in a worktree; the file-chain model already preserves attribution without a message server.
Looking for a message table in skilled bots' runtime: there is none. Delivery entries record where a result went, not what was said.
Looking for an activity view in the status index: it stores rows and flags, not a lifecycle grouping.
Reusing OpenBot's channel/member tables directly. They assume a multi-tenant organization and a database, neither of which this team needs.
Treating the run record as an activity log. It is one record per run; a conversation needs several messages per run.
Adding Better Auth or any identity provider. OpenBot needs it because it serves many organizations over the network; a small team on one host already has an identity in the OS or SSH layer.
Copying the owner/admin/member split. Owner and admin are the same authority in OpenBot's own helper, so the three names collapse to two behaviours, and a few people do not need a delegation tree.
Copying turnstone's permission strings. They exist to let an administrator compose custom roles across endpoints; a small team needs one gate, not a policy language.
Looking for a user table in skilled bots' state root: there is none, only per-identity repository state.
Treating the status index as an identity source: it is keyed by repository identity, not by person.

Building a memory service or embedding store. The reference set's service-shaped memories (OpenBot Intelligence, openhuman CortexDB) exist to serve many users and machines; a few people on one host do not need recall ranking.
Copying OpenBot's per-person Learning containers. They depend on a hosted backend and a skills marketplace; the same value comes from a proposed SKILL.md reviewed in a packet.
Giving each bot its own memory schema. The BOT.md contract is already a stable, small frontmatter; memory belongs beside the bot, not inside its definition.
Reading OpenBot's memory components (`memories.tsx`, `sources.tsx`) for a data model: they are screens over the API, not the model.
Searching skilled bots' runtime for memory code: there is none, and the library README's module table confirms the absence rather than a gap in the search.
Copying OpenBot's goal store and subscription tables. The same behaviour comes from a BOT.md field plus the existing queue, without a database.
Copying the 15-minute floor and 20-enabled cap as server rules. They are product guardrails for a chat-driven authoring surface; a small team authors bots in files and can see the whole list.
Looking for a routine scheduler in skilled bots beyond launchd: cron translation and launchd installation are the whole scheduling layer.
Replaying missed windows. OpenBot's stamp model is better than a backlog, and skilled bots' slot accounting already summarizes missed slots instead of running them.
Treating the queue as a general event bus. It carries run requests with an idempotency key, not arbitrary events.
Building an administrator grant table for apps. With one operator group and a file-defined bot, the bot's own secret allowlist is the grant.
Copying OpenBot's browser computer (live screen, take-the-wheel, recorder). It is the largest surface in OpenBot and the least needed by a team whose bots work in repositories.
Looking for a vault in skilled bots' runtime: secrets come from the process environment and dotenv files, with literal scanning, not from a store.
Looking for an app catalogue in skilled bots: MCP servers are configured outside the bot runtime, in Code Mode's own configuration.
Replacing the worktree with a container per bot. The worktree is cheaper, already audited, and the posture matrix already refuses unsafe combinations.
Building a skill marketplace or a Learning container. Both exist in OpenBot to distribute skills across many people; a small team installs skills by moving a folder.
Giving skills their own storage format. `SKILL.md` with frontmatter already holds everything a proposed skill needs.
Looking for a per-person skill scope in the spec-kit: the packet is the scope, not the person.
Looking for a skill registry in the bots runtime: there is none; skills live in the Skilled tree, and the bot runtime does not read them.
Storing learned skills in the BOT.md body. The body is the standing instruction; a skill is a separate, reviewable, reusable unit.
Adding a separate audit database. The run record, delivery entry and result event already form the trail; a second store would be the first place to drift.

Adding an OpenBot-style action policy engine. A bot's actions happen inside an executor whose sandbox and posture are already enforced; a second policy layer would duplicate the executor's own permission model.
Copying the approvals board as a TUI screen. The board is a filtered list over the inbox; `bots inbox` already lists the same items.
Looking for activity in the status index beyond rows and flags: the index is a summary, not an event log.
Looking for an audit row in skilled bots' run record: the run record has the outcome and evidence, but not a per-decision row.
A "lite" multi-tenant mode. Tenancy is in the URL space and the database schema; a lite version would be a second product.
Adopting the Helm chart as the small-team install path. It installs a cluster workload with a management agent and a licence requirement.
Looking for a mobile web build in the phone app: it is a native React Native project, not a responsive web page.
Looking for a single-user mode in the Kubernetes chart: the personal edition is the single-user mode, and it is explicitly not the chart.
Shipping a mobile client before a terminal client exists. The terminal is the stated preference and the smaller build.
Copying hermes-muse's kernel state machine. It is MIT but Python and coupled to a host plugin API; the state vocabulary is the reusable part, not the code.
Copying OpenBot's React approval cards. The logic is in `shared/`, the cards are presentation tied to the web app.
Copying openhuman-tui code. GPL-3.0-only would force the combined work under GPL.
Looking for a NOTICE file in OpenBot: there is none, so MIT attribution is the only obligation.
Looking for a permissive memory implementation in openhuman: GPL-3.0 rules it out for direct reuse.
A desktop-first build. Iteration 1 found that OpenBot's chat surface is the web app and its Tauri layer is engine and update management.
A server or database for conversations, memory, skills or activity. Each maps to files the runtime already writes, and the queue already provides atomic claims.
Any enterprise, multi-tenant, Kubernetes, managed-upgrade or mobile work (iteration 11).
Looking for one OpenBot component that could be lifted wholesale. The value is distributed across small pure modules and policy documents; the UI is not portable.
Treating the eight parts as independent. Conversations, activity and approvals share the run record and the actor field; building them in the ranked order avoids writing that record three times.

nodes.scope: OpenBot-main/app, OpenBot-main/desktop, OpenMausBot-main, rakazo-main, openhuman-main, turnstone-main, .skilled/bin/bots.cjs
nodes.question: How do OpenBot and the other reference repos give a team conversations with a bot and an activity feed, and can a terminal or TUI match the OpenBot desktop app for that, or is a desktop shell such as Tauri worth adding?

How do approvals work in OpenBot and the other repos, and what is the smallest small-team model of who can talk to, approve for and change a bot, compared with skilled bots' needs-you items and run records?
How does a terminal or TUI present a conversation with a bot together with its approvals, activity and routine list, and which repo's terminal frontend is worth copying?
How are conversations persisted and fanned out so several bots can share one thread, and what is the smallest activity record that can be shown after the fact?
What is the smallest sign-in and role model for a few people sharing one machine or host, and which parts of OpenBot's owner/admin/member split and turnstone's RBAC can be dropped?
How should shared versus per-person memory be scoped when a few people use the same bots, and what does OpenBot's memory model do that skilled bots' per-bot files do not?
